scientific_model.concept: Lamport Logical Clocks: Local Increments and Message Updates
scientific_model.purpose: Teach how a unit-increment logical clock assigns integer timestamps to local events and message receives, and why a smaller timestamp alone does not prove that one event causally preceded another.
scientific_model.focus_alignment: Explain Lamport logical clocks: local events increment a clock and receiving a message updates the receiver to max(local, message timestamp) plus one for a unit-increment implementation. Use small editable integer clocks and show send/receive ordering. Explain that a smaller timestamp does not prove causality. Do not use physical wall-clock time.

assumptions: Each process increments its clock by exactly one per local event (unit increment).
Messages carry the sender's current logical timestamp and are delivered without loss.
limitations: Logical clocks give a partial order; they do not measure real elapsed time or synchronize physical clocks.
The lesson shows one bounded send/receive step, not a full distributed execution or total-order tie-breaking.
misconceptions: A smaller logical timestamp does not prove that the earlier-stamped event caused or happened before the later-stamped event; independent processes can produce timestamps in any relative order.
edge_cases: If the message timestamp is smaller than the receiver's local clock, the receiver still advances to local + 1.
If the message timestamp is larger, the receiver jumps to message + 1, skipping intermediate values.
scientific_model.demonstration_scope: A bounded two-process send/receive trace with integer logical clocks. We compute the receiver's updated clock as max(local, message timestamp) + 1 and compare timestamps. We do not model physical time, clock drift, or full distributed-system synchronization.

lesson_spec.central_learning_question: Teach how a unit-increment logical clock assigns integer timestamps to local events and message receives, and why a smaller timestamp alone does not prove that one event causally preceded another.
learning_objectives: Compute a receiver's updated logical clock from its local clock and an incoming message timestamp using max(local, message) + 1.
Explain why observing timestamp(a) < timestamp(b) does not by itself establish that a happened before b.
audience_prerequisites: Basic integer arithmetic and the max function
Familiarity with the idea of processes exchanging messages
lesson_spec.intuition: Each process keeps a counter. A local event bumps it by one. When a message arrives, the receiver's counter jumps to one more than the larger of its own counter and the message's timestamp, so the receive is stamped after both the send and any earlier local events.

guided_explorations.title: Message timestamp dominates
guided_explorations.change: Set Receiver local clock L to 2; Set Message timestamp M to 7; Set Send event timestamp S to 7.
guided_explorations.observe: Calculated results for this setup, compared with the starting inputs: max(L, M) = 7 (starting value: 5); Updated receiver clock = 8 (starting value: 6); Send timestamp < receive timestamp = true (starting value: true); Receive minus send = 1 (starting value: 1).
guided_explorations.why: When the message timestamp exceeds the local clock, the receiver jumps to message + 1, so the receive is stamped after the send and the gap is one unit.

guided_explorations.title: Local clock dominates
guided_explorations.change: Set Receiver local clock L to 9; Set Message timestamp M to 4; Set Send event timestamp S to 4.
guided_explorations.observe: Calculated results for this setup, compared with the starting inputs: max(L, M) = 9 (starting value: 5); Updated receiver clock = 10 (starting value: 6); Send timestamp < receive timestamp = true (starting value: true); Receive minus send = 6 (starting value: 1).
guided_explorations.why: When the local clock exceeds the message timestamp, the receiver still advances to local + 1, so the receive is stamped after the send even though the message timestamp is smaller.
